key_finding: A field experiment that made an autopay-minimum default less convenient reduced minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged cardholders mostly chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum and some stopped using autopay at all, increasing missed payments.
methodology: Field experiment with card issuer, six-month follow-up on payment behavior and debt outcomes.
why_it_matters: This is the closest real-world proof that a choice-architecture change can move a nominal enrollment/behavior metric while leaving the underlying outcome (debt, and by analogy, saved amount) unchanged or worse \u2014 exactly the 'vanity enrollment' risk our support team is warning about, in an actual consumer banking product rather than a pension.
limitations: studies debt repayment nudges, not savings sign-up
US credit card population, not EU app users
the specific nudge (shrouding) differs from opt-in/opt-out/active choice framing
relevance_reason: Directly tests whether a choice-architecture nudge that changes headline behavior also changes the substantive financial outcome, in a genuine consumer financial product.

key_finding: A state-of-the-art overview of DC plan design covering participation/contribution effects of automatic enrollment and default investment options, including potential negative engagement effects and framing impacts.
methodology: Narrative review/synthesis of the DC retirement plan literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Useful map of the employer-retirement literature the brief flags as the closest analogy, but every finding is filtered through an employer-plan lens that does not carry over to a self-directed consumer app.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not consumer self-directed savings
narrative rather than systematic review
US-centric policy context (SECURE 2.0)
relevance_reason: Broad synthesis of default and plan-design effects in the analogous but non-transferable employer-retirement setting.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises short-term retirement participation but induces passivity \u2014 low contribution rates, non-management of accounts, account churn \u2014 so enrollment alone does not establish welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative policy-oriented review of default enrollment in US retirement plans. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Restates the support team's disengagement concern in the employer-pension literature, but offers no consumer-app-specific evidence or effect sizes.
limitations: employer retirement plans, not consumer savings app
no quantitative effect sizes given
recommendations (auto-escalation, re-enrollment) are pension-specific
relevance_reason: Articulates the 'passive trap' concern the brief's support team raises, in the retirement-plan literature.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior over time, identifying time course, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators, and sets a research agenda to reconcile inconsistent findings.
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical review synthesizing the consumer-default literature; no new empirical data. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: This is the review the brief asks for on the persistence question: it gives the conceptual machinery for predicting when a default's effect on enrollment will or won't persist into actual saved amounts, directly informing what to measure at 6-12 months and why heterogeneity matters.
limitations: conceptual/taxonomic, not a quantitative meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
not specific to financial products
abstract-only, no numeric estimates
relevance_reason: General consumer-behavior review addressing exactly the downstream persistence and heterogeneity questions the brief poses, without the employer-pension framing.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive to the value of the default option even when it causes substantial losses; variation in active choice is driven by transitory shocks, not attentiveness.
methodology: Three natural experiments including random assignment to default options in a large administrative health-insurance dataset.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that default adherence can be near-total and insensitive to stakes, which bears on whether an opt-out round-up default would be sticky regardless of quality \u2014 but the setting is health-insurance choice, not a consumer financial product.
limitations: health insurance enrollment, not consumer savings
no employer intermediary but also no financial-product framing
no direct evidence on amount saved or preset-level anchoring
relevance_reason: Rigorous evidence on default persistence and insensitivity to value, in a non-employer but off-domain (health insurance) setting.

key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation once job turnover, pre-vesting withdrawals, and opt-outs from escalation are accounted for; only 40% of those defaulted into auto-escalation actually escalate on the first date.
methodology: Longitudinal administrative analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: naive enrollment-lift numbers substantially overstate the real, medium-run increase in money saved once attrition and opt-out are accounted for.
limitations: retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated context the brief says doesn't transfer
no direct measure of engagement or complaints
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that default enrollment reliably translates into materially more saving, with quantified effect sizes.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees into a public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most affected individuals actively opted out; the default effect was stronger when incentives were higher and knowledge of enrollment status was lower.
methodology: Natural policy experiment using linked administrative and survey data on a nationwide pension auto-enrollment rollout.
why_it_matters: Shows default strength is conditional on incentive salience and awareness, informing how much enrollment lift to expect and for whom, but in a locked, government pension rather than liquid consumer product.
limitations: pension savings, not liquid consumer savings
government/employer-adjacent mechanism
no medium-term persistence data beyond opt-out decision
relevance_reason: Quantifies default effect size and its dependence on incentives/awareness in a non-US pension-default setting.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, with only modest average savings increases at the longer horizon though inequality in savings is reduced; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly addresses the brief's 6-12+ month persistence question with quantified attenuation, reinforcing that enrollment-rate effects overstate medium-run savings gains, but the setting is employer retirement plans.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a liquid consumer product
structural model relies on strong life-cycle assumptions
no distributional analysis by engagement or complaints
relevance_reason: Quantifies how default effects on enrollment decay over medium horizons, closely paralleling the brief's persistence question in the analogous but off-domain pension setting.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default (or having it refused) lowers ratings of the advisor's honesty and advice quality, and how the default is framed and presented also shifts the chosen allocation.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments, one large representative multi-country European sample, on default framing in investment/wealth-management decisions.
why_it_matters: Gives EU consumer-context evidence that defaults can anchor the chosen level (relevant to the preset-multiplier decision) while also measurably damaging perceived trust when a default is imposed or refused \u2014 the exact 'dark pattern' reputational risk the brief flags.
limitations: wealth-management advice context, not a round-up savings app
risk-taking allocation rather than a savings-amount outcome
no medium/long-term persistence data
relevance_reason: EU-based experimental evidence on default framing effects on chosen level and on perceived manipulation, directly speaking to the brief's dark-pattern concern.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate (2-3%) and a conservative default fund, and half still held the default rate/fund even after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms analyzing 401(k) participation, default acceptance, and asset accumulation.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a preset level anchors most people's contribution choice for years, which is the strongest historical evidence for the brief's anchoring concern about the multiplier decision, but the brief explicitly says this foundational pension literature is dated relative to app/regulatory context.
limitations: classic employer 401k study explicitly deprioritized by the brief as foundational rather than current
no year metadata given, likely predates the regulatory/app context
retirement savings, not liquid consumer savings
relevance_reason: Foundational anchoring-on-default-level evidence that current work in this scan argues with.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost (84% of adherence needs both), and a counterfactual adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20/25/30% menu would capture 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on large-scale transaction data plus an independent stated-preference survey to identify true preferences.
why_it_matters: The closest available quantitative precedent for the preset-multiplier decision: it shows how a menu of preset options (analogous to 1x/2x/5x) anchors choice through friction rather than reshaping preference, and quantifies the welfare cost/benefit of adding or changing menu options \u2014 directly informing what levels to preset and whether an empty field would perform differently.
limitations: tipping decisions, not savings contributions
consumer payment app setting, not a savings product specifically
no persistence or long-run engagement outcomes
relevance_reason: Directly analogous structural evidence on how preset menu options anchor consumer choice, in a self-directed digital consumer payment setting.

key_finding: An opt-in short-term (anytime-withdrawal) payroll savings program at five UK firms saw excellent retention among adopters \u2014 96% still held a balance and 87% still received an automatic contribution after 12 months \u2014 but take-up was extremely low, with at most 0.7% of eligible employees ever activating an account.
methodology: Field study of the rollout of an opt-in liquid, anytime-withdrawal savings account program across five UK employers.
why_it_matters: This is the closest product-structure match to the round-up feature (liquid, withdraw-anytime savings, not retirement) and shows opt-in alone can produce vanishingly small enrollment despite the product working well for those who adopt it \u2014 direct evidence against relying on opt-in for the entry decision.
limitations: delivered via employer payroll, not a standalone consumer app
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice enrollment in this study
UK employer sample, not EU consumer banking app users
relevance_reason: Uniquely close product analog (liquid, anytime-withdrawal savings) showing opt-in enrollment failure despite strong retention among adopters.

key_finding: A general theoretical characterization shows that when designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions to Pigouvian fees and cases of normative disagreement, verified via numerical simulation.
methodology: Theoretical mechanism-design model with asymptotic approximations, validated by numerical simulation. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides a normative framework for when defaulting everyone in (vs. active choice) is welfare-optimal, which is conceptually relevant to justifying the entry-mechanism decision, though it offers no empirical numbers from any real product.
limitations: purely theoretical/abstract, no empirical validation in any real setting
assumes designer-chooser value agreement, uncertain for our app
no population or setting specified
relevance_reason: General normative theory of optimal default design that could justify or challenge an opt-out choice on welfare grounds.

key_finding: EU law regulates dark patterns as violations of consumer autonomy, and the article develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations (including pre-selected defaults) to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from regulable manipulation.
methodology: Legal/normative analysis mapping EU dark-pattern law and constructing an autonomy-violation taxonomy. abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the specific EU legal framework for judging whether an opt-out entry design would read as a regulable dark pattern versus a helpful default, directly addressing the brief's EU reputational-risk constraint.
limitations: Legal/normative analysis, not empirical evidence on enrolment or savings behaviour
No effect sizes or behavioural outcomes
relevance_reason: Supplies the EU dark-pattern/autonomy framework the brief explicitly asks for when weighing opt-out against active choice.

key_finding: A 12% default contribution rate left 25% of employees still at the default after 12 months (vs. ~50% typically remaining at lower defaults per a literature review), and defaulted employees had systematically lower income than predicted, implying anchoring at a suboptimal level.
methodology: Retrospective analysis of one large 401(k) plan's 12% automatic-enrollment default compared against a literature review of lower-default plans. abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether the preset level anchors the final contribution and shows the anchor binds hardest on low-income employees, the core evidence needed for the C3 anchoring question, even though set in a pension plan.
limitations: Employer-sponsored 401(k) plan, not a consumer app
Abstract gives partial rather than complete effect sizes
relevance_reason: Best evidence in the shortlist on whether a high preset default anchors final contribution levels and who is disproportionately affected.

key_finding: Abstract text is corrupted/unavailable ("Trant"), so no usable finding can be extracted despite the title's promise of four large U.K. experiments on automating short-term payroll savings.
methodology: abstract-only; abstract text is not usable.
why_it_matters: The title suggests a closer analogue (short-term, non-retirement automated savings) than the pension literature, but with no legible abstract it cannot currently inform the entry or level decisions.
limitations: Abstract is unusable/corrupted
Cannot verify claimed effect sizes, persistence, or setting
relevance_reason: Potentially the closest analogue to round-up savings automation, but its content cannot be evaluated from the available abstract.

key_finding: Large-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though alerts only capture less than half of consumers' potential savings.
methodology: At-scale randomized field experiments run at major UK banks.
why_it_matters: Shows that automatic enrollment into a real consumer-banking-app feature produces quantified, real behaviour change rather than only nominal sign-up, the closest available evidence bearing on whether opt-out enrolment into round-ups would move actual financial behaviour.
limitations: Overdraft alerts, not a savings/round-up product
No 6-12 month persistence data reported in the abstract
relevance_reason: Closest real consumer-banking-app auto-enrollment field experiment with quantified effect sizes, directly analogous to the round-up feature's opt-out design.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment into UK pensions raises average pension savings (£32-38/month) but this gain is partly offset by increases in unsecured debt (£7/month) and mortgage balances over 41 months, though loan defaults fall and credit scores rise modestly.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment from the randomized roll-out of automatic enrollment pensions to ~160,000 UK employers with 2-29 employees.
why_it_matters: Warns that default-driven savings gains can be partly financed by offsetting debt rather than representing pure net saving, a welfare caveat relevant to judging whether round-up 'savings' constitute real gains.
limitations: Employer pension plan, not a liquid consumer savings product
Debt-offset mechanism may not scale down to small round-up sums
relevance_reason: Cautionary long-run evidence that auto-enrollment savings gains can be partly illusory once offsetting debt behaviour is considered.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrollment 'ordeal' (extra step) to a health-insurance auto-enrollment policy reduced enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying the removal/addition of an auto-enrollment step in a public health-insurance program, with a supporting adverse-selection model.
why_it_matters: Shows that adding friction such as an active-choice step does not fall evenly across the population, disproportionately excluding disadvantaged groups, a direct warning for the distributional cost of requiring active choice.
limitations: Health insurance selection market, not consumer savings
An 'ordeal' extra step is not identical to an active-choice screen
relevance_reason: Strong distributional evidence that enrolment friction differentially excludes vulnerable groups, relevant to weighing active choice's hidden costs.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million while also increasing refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller, less-experienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting different rollout timing of pre-checked recurring-donation defaults across 2020 U.S. campaign websites.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the mechanism the brief's support team worries about: a default creating an unintended recurring commitment lifts nominal sign-up but generates disproportionate refunds/complaints among smaller, less experienced users, the clearest quantified analogue to round-up opt-out risk.
limitations: Political donations, not a savings product
No 6-12 month engagement or withdrawal outcomes reported
relevance_reason: Best-quantified real-world evidence of a recurring-commitment default producing both enrolment gains and manipulation-like backlash, closely analogous to the round-up opt-out risk.

key_finding: In a lab search experiment, defaults raise reservation utility via a reference effect leading to better choices, while agents who reject the default and search actively are more likely to find superior options through self-selection.
methodology: Theoretical search model with reference-dependent utility, tested in laboratory choice experiments with search costs and a default option.
why_it_matters: Offers a general behavioural mechanism for why defaults and active search interact, but stays at the level of generic lab economics rather than financial-product enrolment.
limitations: Generic laboratory search task, not a financial or consumer-app setting
No enrolment or amount-saved outcomes
relevance_reason: General theoretical mechanism for default vs. active-choice effects, useful only as background.

key_finding: After the EU Digital Markets Act mandated active-choice browser screens replacing preset defaults, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting 15+ months after rollout.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered rollout of EU DMA-mandated choice screens on iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale, long-horizon evidence that a regulator-mandated active-choice screen can substantially and durably shift outcomes away from a preset default in a digital consumer product, directly informing whether active choice would meaningfully move enrolment relative to opt-in/opt-out and whether the effect fades.
limitations: Browser choice, not a financial savings product
Measures usage share, not amount saved or engagement depth
relevance_reason: The strongest available evidence on active choice versus default persistence at scale in an EU-regulated consumer digital product, directly bearing on the entry-design decision.

key_finding: In a usability study with 410 participants, generalizable active opt-out schemes (extending one choice to a broader set without a default) reduced disruption, with the least disruptive scheme leaving 98% of participants feeling undisrupted (a 40-point improvement over baseline) while 83% understood the mechanism and made intentional choices.
methodology: Design and usability study of nine active-choice (no-default) interface schemes implemented in a browser extension, tested with 410 participants.
why_it_matters: Provides concrete interface-design lessons for making a required active-choice onboarding step low-friction and legally robust without relying on a default, informing how to implement active choice well rather than whether to use it.
limitations: Privacy opt-out setting, not financial enrolment
No enrolment-rate or savings-amount outcomes
relevance_reason: Offers interface-design evidence for building a low-friction active-choice mechanism relevant to implementing the active-choice option.

key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased sign-ups, but for outcomes requiring effort (exam completion/passing), gains were concentrated among 'responsive' students who would likely have signed up anyway, with no effect on target outcomes for non-responsive individuals.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up defaults to opt-out across university study programs, comparing responsive vs. non-responsive students.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the brief's central worry in a structurally similar effortful-task setting: opt-out lifts nominal sign-up but effortful downstream follow-through only improves for people who would have opted in anyway, so the enrolment lift can be a vanity metric for the passively enrolled.
limitations: University exam sign-up, not a financial product
No monetary outcome analogous to amount saved
relevance_reason: Structurally close analogy to the brief's core disengagement worry: defaults raise sign-up but not effortful follow-through for non-responsive people.

key_finding: After the Pension Protection Act allowed target-date funds as default options, younger workers defaulted into TDFs invested more in stocks and older workers less, matching the glidepath, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of U.S. retirement investors from 2006-2018, exploiting the PPA default-option policy change.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can strongly shape a downstream allocation choice without moving contribution rates, a weak analogy for whether presetting the round-up multiplier would anchor the amount saved without changing enrolment.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plan, not liquid consumer savings
Concerns investment allocation, not enrolment or engagement
relevance_reason: Minor supporting evidence that defaults shape allocation-type choices but not contribution levels, tangential to the anchoring question.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving decisions in China, behavioural nudges including default options significantly reduced willingness to contribute and the share of income allocated to saving, contrary to prevailing international evidence, with the largest backfire effects for positive-narrative and default-option nudges.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions (n=220).
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's working assumption that defaults reliably lift enrolment, the most explicit counter-evidence in the shortlist that a default can backfire and reduce contribution, with heterogeneity by income, education, and gender.
limitations: Hypothetical online-survey decisions rather than a live product
Small sample (n=220) and a non-EU, non-fintech cultural context (China)
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the set, directly answering the brief's request for a paper contesting the 'defaults always help' premise.

key_finding: People generally approve of financial nudges/interventions, with strongest approval for those framed around savings and targeting deliberate (System 2) rather than automatic (System 1) processing; younger, female, urban, higher-income respondents favor them most.
methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment; 2,100 representative Australian respondents rated 36 hypothetical financial intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing (spending vs. saving), and System (1 vs. 2) on approval, ethics, manipulation, and likelihood of use.
why_it_matters: Suggests our round-up feature should be framed in savings terms and lean toward deliberate/System-2 mechanisms (favoring active choice over covert opt-out) to be seen as helpful rather than manipulative — directly informs the messaging and framing around whichever entry design we choose.
limitations: hypothetical vignette approval, not actual enrollment or savings behavior
Australian sample rather than EU regulatory context
self-reported approval may not predict real complaint or withdrawal behavior
relevance_reason: Directly tests when a financial default/nudge is perceived as manipulative vs. beneficial, the exact reputational-risk question the brief raises.

key_finding: Offering conditional cash transfer beneficiaries the choice between cash and bank-account transfer had no significant average effect on savings, but increased balances for those with previously nonpositive savings.
methodology: Field experiment among CCT beneficiaries comparing cash disbursement vs. bank-account delivery, tracking downstream savings and trust outcomes.
why_it_matters: Suggests account-based delivery mainly helps people with no prior savings habit, a distributional finding tangential to our enrollment/level decisions but in a population and product far removed from a consumer round-up feature.
limitations: developing-country CCT population, not EU consumer banking app users
not about opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrollment mechanics
no default effect sizes given
relevance_reason: Offers distributional evidence on who benefits from savings-account defaults, but in an unrelated welfare-transfer setting.

key_finding: Abstract fragment discusses liquid-fund withdrawal rules in an automatic IRA with an emergency-savings feature but provides no interpretable results.
methodology: abstract-only; text is incomplete and does not describe design or findings clearly.
why_it_matters: Emergency-savings-linked accounts are conceptually adjacent to a liquid round-up pot, but the abstract gives no usable evidence for our enrollment or level decisions.
limitations: abstract is a fragment lacking findings
employer/IRA context rather than consumer app
no effect sizes reported
relevance_reason: Nominally about automatic IRA emergency savings, a design analog, but abstract supplies no usable evidence.

key_finding: Switching from opt-in to automatic 401(k) enrollment dramatically raised participation, and most auto-enrolled employees stuck with both the default contribution rate and default investment allocation.
methodology: Before/after natural experiment using administrative payroll and plan data from one large U.S. corporation.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a default shapes both whether people enroll and the level they end up at — the mechanism underlying our multiplier-anchoring concern — but it's an employer plan, so the trusted-intermediary mechanism doesn't carry over cleanly.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k), not a self-directed consumer app
2001 data, predates current app/UX and EU regulatory context
single-firm case study
relevance_reason: Closest classic precedent for default anchoring on enrollment and contribution level, though set in employer retirement plans.

key_finding: No abstract available; title indicates a comparison of savings behaviors between automatic and voluntary enrollment in a defined contribution retirement plan.
methodology: abstract-only; no content provided.
why_it_matters: Potentially relevant title but no extractable evidence for our decisions given the missing abstract.
limitations: no abstract text available
employer DC retirement plan context, not consumer app
relevance_reason: Title suggests direct relevance to auto vs. voluntary enrollment, but no abstract content to extract evidence from.

key_finding: Limited trust in financial institutions and minority/non-national status are both associated with lower voluntary pension contributions and higher rates of early withdrawal after a pension-freedom reform.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) surrounding a policy reform introducing an early-withdrawal option to a mandatory pension scheme.
why_it_matters: Shows the same low-trust population that under-saves voluntarily is also most likely to withdraw early once given freedom to exit — a distributional warning echoing the support team's fear that passively enrolled or easily-exiting users disengage and withdraw quickly.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme population, not a voluntary consumer savings app
Estonian institutional context differs from EU banking-app users
no direct measure of opt-in/opt-out enrollment-default effect
relevance_reason: Distributional evidence on who under-saves and withdraws early, relevant to who is helped vs. hurt by enrollment design, though in a mandatory pension setting.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrollment nudge policy reduced stated intentions to comply and decreased approval of the policy.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries manipulating reflection on a hypothetical automatic-enrollment nudge for vaccine boosters.
why_it_matters: Shows that making a default's mechanism salient can backfire into disapproval and reduced compliance — a caution for how we communicate opt-out enrollment or exit options to avoid triggering the 'dark pattern' backlash the brief worries about.
limitations: vaccination policy setting, not financial savings
hypothetical intentions rather than realized enrollment or savings behavior
no measure of actual behavior change, only stated intent/approval
relevance_reason: Directly relevant to when a default is perceived as manipulative and triggers backlash, despite being in a non-financial domain.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment and employer-matching provisions are associated with higher likelihood of retirement-plan participation among U.S. Millennials in the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study.
methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study with regression controls for income, debt, and risk tolerance.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the well-known auto-enrollment participation effect in a modern cohort but adds little beyond the foundational employer-plan literature and doesn't touch persistence, amount saved, or active-choice comparisons.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not self-directed consumer product
cross-sectional survey data, no persistence or amount-saved measure
correlational, not causal design
relevance_reason: Confirms auto-enrollment's participation effect in employer plans, redundant with stronger foundational studies and off our target setting.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic employer retirement contributions substantially raised wealth accumulation, while tax subsidies requiring active choice mainly shifted assets between accounts (only ~1 cent of extra saving per $1 spent), with just ~15% of individuals being active responders.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel-data analysis of the full Danish population's retirement savings accounts.
why_it_matters: The strongest evidence that passive/default mechanisms change real saved amounts for the inattentive majority, while active-choice/subsidy approaches mainly reshuffle money among the financially sophisticated minority — a critical caution against assuming active choice alone raises real savings.
limitations: Danish tax-advantaged retirement accounts, not a liquid consumer savings app
employer-mediated automatic contributions rather than app-based opt-out design
does not address multiplier-level anchoring in a round-up feature
relevance_reason: Landmark distributional evidence on active vs. passive savers and whether defaults change real saved amounts, the exact question the brief poses, though in a retirement/tax-advantaged setting.

key_finding: Field experiments show that requiring an explicit choice ('active choice'), and especially an 'enhanced active choice' that highlights the losses of not choosing the preferred option, can motivate behavior change as an alternative or complement to automatic-enrollment defaults.
methodology: Review of prior default/active-choice literature plus two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice interventions.
why_it_matters: Introduces and validates the active-choice design that is one of the brief's two open decisions, plus a specific 'enhanced' variant (highlighting the cost of opting out) we could adapt for our forced-choice onboarding screen to capture more enrollment benefit without full passive opt-out.
limitations: primarily tested in medication-adherence/health contexts; financial savings application discussed but not directly field-tested here
abstract gives no numeric effect sizes
2011 paper, predates current app/regulatory context
relevance_reason: Directly introduces and tests the active-choice and enhanced-active-choice designs central to the brief's first open decision.

key_finding: This chapter synthesizes household-finance research on consumption/saving, choice architecture, and product-design interventions (education, defaults, advice, disclosure) that shape financial behavior.
methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter summarizing empirical regularities and behavioral interventions in household finance.
why_it_matters: Provides the broader map of choice-architecture tools beyond defaults and situates default effects among alternatives like disclosure or advice, supplying the synthesis-level context the brief asked for beyond a single study.
limitations: narrative overview, not a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
covers mostly employer retirement and general household finance rather than a fintech round-up product specifically
no quantitative effect sizes in the abstract
relevance_reason: The broad review/synthesis of behavioral household-finance interventions the brief calls for, situating default and choice-architecture effects in context.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation above 85% at three large firms, but about half of participants still held the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default fund even after three years.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing automatic vs. opt-in enrollment cohorts.
why_it_matters: The clearest classic demonstration that default enrollment persists for years but also anchors contribution levels durably — warns us that whichever multiplier we pre-select in the round-up feature is likely to become the long-run norm for many users, so the level choice matters as much as the entry mechanism.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, not a self-directed consumer savings app
early-2000s data, before current app/UX and EU regulatory context
three firms only, limited generalizability
relevance_reason: Best classic evidence that default enrollment and preset contribution levels persist and anchor behavior for years, directly informing the level-anchoring concern even though set in employer plans.

key_finding: Randomly assigning employees to default enrollment in a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points — equivalent to a 50% savings match — driven by present bias and the cognitive cost of evaluating alternatives; the default also increased later voluntary active saving.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among salaried employees in Afghanistan testing several variants of a salary-linked savings account default.
why_it_matters: Offers a rare mechanistic explanation for why defaults work (present bias, decision cost) and shows defaults can increase later voluntary engagement rather than only passive enrollment, useful for predicting how a mobile round-up default might affect present-biased users.
limitations: employer/salary-linked savings account rather than a fully self-directed consumer app
Afghan context very different from EU consumer regulatory and liquidity setting
abstract gives no long-run (6-12 month) retention detail beyond study conclusion
relevance_reason: Provides mechanistic evidence for why default enrollment increases participation, relevant to predicting default effectiveness, though set in an employer/developing-country context.

key_finding: A field experiment with payment reminders reduced credit card late fees by 14% but increased overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil; fee outcomes tracked across credit card and checking accounts.
why_it_matters: Gives quantified evidence that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while making a specific, identifiable subgroup worse off — directly bears on the brief's requirement not to ship a default that looks good on average while harming vulnerable users, and argues for monitoring heterogeneous effects (e.g. by liquidity/overdraft history) rather than a single enrolment metric.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
credit card/overdraft fee context rather than round-up savings
no data on persistence beyond the fee-measurement period
relevance_reason: Best available quantified evidence in this batch for the brief's explicit concern about who is helped versus hurt by a nudge in a consumer financial product.
